notes:
I found good verse-by-verse material for Numbers 13, but there are clear gaps. I found **nothing from the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Pentecostal-denominational or prosperity/word-of-faith sites**, so those sections are left out. Also, **the traditions don't really disagree here.** Reformed (Calvin, Henry), Baptist (Gill), Wesleyan (Clarke, Benson) and Calvary Chapel teachers (Guzik, Chuck Smith) all read the chapter the same way: ten spies walked by sight, two by faith. The only real debates are (a) whether sending spies was wrong in the first place, and (b) what "Nephilim" means. I've marked these where they come up.

---

**vv. 1–3: The command to send spies**
- Deut 1:22 shows the idea came from the people, and Matthew Henry calls it the fruit of their unbelief. In his view God told Moses to go along with the request, but God bore no share in the sin that followed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_013.cfm
- Guzik points out that God had already searched out the land (Ezek 20:6). Moses may have been wrong to agree, but in the bigger picture God used the mission to test Israel's faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-13/
- Mattoon (on Precept Austin) is sharper: sending spies wasn't God's perfect or original plan, and it showed fear and a lack of faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-13-commentary
- Coffman agrees that asking for spies showed a lack of faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/numbers-13.html
- **Where readings differ:** The Pulpit Commentary says Numbers and Deut 1 don't contradict each other; they show the same events from different angles. In its view God took over the people's request because it was better for their hidden disloyalty to come out before they entered the land. It adds that the twelve were not the tribal princes but well-known, probably younger men. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-13.html
- Calvin also deals with the Deut 1 tension. He says Deuteronomy puts all the blame on the people because Moses' aim there was to convict them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-13.html

**vv. 4–15: The names**
- One man came from each tribe so that the whole nation was represented. Guzik notes that Caleb's name sounds like the Hebrew word for "dog," and cites Allen, who takes it in an honourable sense. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-13/
- Calvin says the ten names are recorded as a lasting reminder of their disgrace. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-13.html
- Henry reports a view that all twelve are named for the sake of the two good ones. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-13.html
- Pulpit: none of these names appears elsewhere except Caleb and Joshua. Levi sent no spy because it had no claim to territory. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-13.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: comparing the names shows none of the twelve tribal princes went. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-13.html
- v. 6: Pulpit discusses Caleb being called "the Kenezite" elsewhere. It thinks the likeness to the Kenizzite people is probably a coincidence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-13.html

**v. 16: Hoshea renamed Joshua**
- NET note: the change is small, from "he saves" to "the LORD saves." The Greek Old Testament renders the name *Iesoun* (Jesus). https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Num+13%3A8%2C16
- Guzik says the new name is the Hebrew form of "Jesus." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-13/
- Gill and Henry both see Joshua as a type (foreshadowing) of Christ, citing Heb 4:8 and Matt 1:21. Joshua saved Israel from the powers of Canaan; Christ saves from the powers of hell. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/13-16.html
- Pulpit notes a difficulty: Joshua is already called by the new name in Exod 17:9. Either those earlier uses look ahead, or the name had changed earlier and the spy list was copied from tribal records. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-13.html

**vv. 17–20: Moses' instructions**
- Guzik sees a hint of unbelief, as if the spies were checking whether God described the land truthfully, though he calls it reasonable. Asking whether the people were "strong or weak" was risky either way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-13/
- Pulpit says Moses was guilty of "some indiscretion" here: the enemy's strength shouldn't have mattered, since God was giving the land. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-13.html
- Ripe grapes: Wenham (quoted by Guzik) says late July. Pulpit agrees. Clarke suggests the spies left in early August and returned mid-September. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/numbers-13.html

**v. 21: The route**
- Pulpit: the Wilderness of Zin was the southern border. Rehob was probably Beth-rehob near the later city of Dan, on the road to Hamath. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-13.html
- Jensen: the trip ran from the far south to the far north. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-13-commentary

**v. 22: Hebron, Anak's descendants, Zoan**
- Guzik: Hebron held the patriarchs' tombs, yet the spies don't mention them. Allen says the spies were too busy with "sandal sizes" to remember the promise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-13/
- Constable: God had promised Abraham the land near Hebron. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-13-commentary
- "Seven years before Zoan": Gill and Poole say this was meant to humble Egypt's boast about how old its cities were. Barnes suggests the Hyksos built both cities. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/13-22.html
- Pulpit: Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai may have been clans rather than individuals. It thinks Moses got the date from Egyptian records or priests. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-13.html

**vv. 23–24: The Eshcol cluster**
- Why two men on a pole? Clarke, Pulpit and Gill say it was to keep the grapes from being crushed, not because of the weight. Keil & Delitzsch think it was the cluster's extraordinary size. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-13.html
- Clarke and Gill think Joshua and Caleb probably carried it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/13-23.html
- Ellicott: the valley may have been named earlier after Eshcol, Abraham's ally. Pulpit agrees and says the place got a new meaning for an old name. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-13.html
- A homiletical commentary reads the fruit as a foretaste of heaven, in which Jesus is seen. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/numbers-13.html

**v. 25: Forty days**
- Guzik: about 250 miles, and forty is often a number of testing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-13/
- Pulpit: the number shows the land was fully explored. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-13.html

**vv. 26–27: The return and "milk and honey"**
- Mattoon sees Kadesh as a place of failure. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-13-commentary
- Guzik: saying "where *you* sent us" suggests the spies felt they were on Israel's mission, not God's. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-13/
- Henry: even the bad spies had to admit the land was fruitful. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_013.cfm
- Calvin: the ten opened with honest facts so they could deceive more effectively afterwards. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-13.html

**vv. 28–29: "Nevertheless"**
- Guzik: the word means "despite all that." The report admits God's promise is true and still says it can't be done. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-13/
- Jensen: the word shows the spies' pessimism leaking into the report. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-13-commentary
- Pulpit: Moses himself had pointed them to the people's strength, and now they dwelt on nothing else. The Amalekites were roaming bands, not settled Canaanites. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-13.html

**v. 30: Caleb**
- Precept Austin: Caleb was hushing the whole crowd, not just the ten spies. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-13-commentary
- Why isn't Joshua named? Pulpit suggests that, as Moses' assistant, he stepped back so Caleb could speak as a more neutral witness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-13.html
- Coffman: Caleb's confidence was in God, not in himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/numbers-13.html

**v. 31: "Stronger than we"**
- Guzik: true from a human point of view, but a lie to say they couldn't go up. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-13/
- Pulpit: Israel clearly had more people. The real fears were walled cities and giants in an age of hand-to-hand fighting. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-13.html

**v. 32: "Devours its inhabitants"**
- Pulpit: this can't mean famine or disease, which would contradict their own report. It means constant wars and invasions. "All" the people being huge is an exaggeration. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-13.html
- Barnes agrees the land was always exposed to attack. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/13-33.htm
- Precept Austin: the report was "evil" because it exaggerated, spread fear, and showed no faith in God's promise. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-13-commentary
- A homiletical commentary: a report can be true in its facts and still be false and evil in its spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/numbers-13.html

**v. 33: Nephilim and grasshoppers (the main debated point)**
- Ellicott: it's the same word as in Gen 6:4. https://biblehub.com/numbers/13-33.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch take Nephilim as "primeval tyrants." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/13-33.html
- Pulpit is doubtful. It's not certain the Nephilim were giants, and very unlikely the Anakim were actually connected to them; the spies' fear revived the old name. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-13.html
- Bible Hub's study note leaves it open: a literal claim of ancestry, or language shaped by terror. https://biblehub.com/study/numbers/13-33.htm
- One note on Bible Hub says the "descendants of Anak" aside was probably added later by a scribe. The page doesn't clearly say who wrote it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/13-33.htm
- "Grasshoppers": Gill and Benson (Wesleyan) call it an exaggeration born of fear. Gill adds that the spies couldn't really have known how the giants saw them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/13-33.htm
- F. B. Meyer: the spies got "God, giant, grasshopper" in the wrong order. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-13-commentary

---

**Other views (modern scholarship)**
- Coffman quotes the older critical view that the chapter combines two sources, JE and P, which disagree on the route and on whether Joshua was involved. He rejects it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/numbers-13.html
- Keil & Delitzsch also argue against that view. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-13.html
- NET note (via Precept Austin): Zoan is probably Tanis, though some scholars dispute this. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-13-commentary

**Catholic translation only:** The Douay-Rheims calls the Anakim "monsters… of the giant kind" and names Zoan as Tanis. I found no Catholic commentary on these verses. https://biblehub.com/numbers/13-22.htm
